chunks: Al-Husayn ibn Muhammad from Mu'alla ibn Muhammad from Al-Hasan ibn Ali from Ahmad ibn A'iz from Abu Salama from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) said:

Regarding two slave men, to whom it was delegated that they buy and sell with their own wealth, so there was a dispute between them. So this one went running to the master of that one, and that one ran to the master of this one, and they were equal in strength. So this one bought that slave from his master, and that one went and bought the other slave from his master, and they returned to their place, and each one of them clung to his companion and said to him, 'You are my slave, as I have bought you from your master.'

He (peace be upon him) said: 'Judgement is made between them from where they separated; the path is measured. So whichever of the two was closer, he is the one who preceded the one who was further. And if they were equal, then it is a return to their masters; they came equally and separated equally, except if one of the two preceded his companion, then the predecessor is entitled to him; if he wishes, he sells him, and if he wishes, he keeps him, and it is not for him to harm him by it.'
And in another report, he (peace be upon him) said: 'When the distance is equal, a lot is drawn between them, so whichever of the two the lot falls on, he becomes his slave.'
ai.seo_question: How is ownership determined when two competing slaves buy each other?
ai.summary: This ruling from al-Kafi addresses the specific fiqh of 'buying oneself' through mutual agreement, establishing that ownership is determined by physical proximity to the starting point, with lot-drawing as a tie-breaker. It reflects the practical legal mechanisms of the Abbasid era regarding slave autonomy and property rights, ensuring clarity in ownership disputes without imposing undue burden on the newly acquired slave.

en.hubeali:
Al Husayn Bin Muhammad, from Moalla Bin Muhammad, from Al Hassan Bin Ali, from Ahmad Bin A’iz, from Abu Salama, 
(It has been narrated) from Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup>

having said regarding two men who were owned slaves, the buying and selling having been authorised by their two masters, so there was a (heated) discussion between the two. So this one went out running to the master of that one, and that one ran to the the master of this one, and they were both equal in strength. So this one bought that slave from his master, and that one went and bought this other slave from his master, and they both left to go to their place, and each one of the two clung to his companions and said to him, ‘You are my slave, as I have bought you from your master’.

He<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘The judgement between the two is from where they separated, a measurement of the street. So whichever of the two was closer so he is the one who preceded the one who was further; and if both were equidistant, so they would both be returned to their relevant masters, having come equally and being equidistant, except if one of the two happens to have preceded his companions, so the first one, it would be for him, if he so desires to he sells, and if he so desires to he keeps, and it is not for him that he harms him by it’.
And in another report, ‘(He<sup>asws</sup> said): ‘When the route was the same (in distance), a lot would be drawn between the two, so whichever of the two the lot falls with, would be his slave’.
en.sarwar: 3. Al-Husayn from Muhammad has narrated from Mu’alla’ ibn Muhammad from al-Hassan ibn Ali from Ahmad ibn ‘A’idh from abu Salmah who has said the following:

“About the case of two slaves who belong to two people and each is authorized to buy and sell with their properties. The two slaves disagree on something and each one runs to the other’s owner, both of equal physical strength, and buy the other slave from his master. They return to their place each with the claim of buying the other from his master and each says, ‘You are my slave because I have bought you from your master.’

Abu ‘Abd Allah, ‘Alayhi al-Salam, has said, ‘From the place they separate from each other the distance is measured, then whoever was closer is the winner. If the distance is the same then whoever has reached the master of the other faster is the winner. He can then sell the other or keep, as he likes, but he cannot beat him up.’
In another Hadith it is said that if the distance is the same the case is decided by casting raffle to find out who is the winner.’”
